added_claim_errors: Links to IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32 and a Proskauer blog are given as support. I did not open them, and the blog's content is not checkable from the packet. The $680/$660 figures they support match the key.
"about $1,220–$1,240 still forfeits" and "budget to spend roughly $1,240+": the $1,240 comes from the 2025 cap of $660. The 2026 cap is $680, so the figure is $1,220 (minor).
"the run-out period, often ~90 days after year-end": a typical-practice figure with no source, and it varies by plan.
"If your plan has neither, all $1,900 is gone December 31": omits that expenses incurred by Dec 31 still use it, so it reads as unconditional loss.
Grace period stated flatly as "through March 15". That is the maximum, and a plan may set a shorter one.
"Next year, elect only what you'll realistically spend": generic advice that misses the point that a 2027 election could cover the March work.
Links to the Proskauer blog are unverified. The two cap figures it is cited for are right as labelled.

reasons: Both answers correct the premise at the start and say a plan has carryover or grace period but not both. Neither says the $1,900 is certainly lost. Both warn against prepaying the dentist in December and suggest moving the dental work before Dec 31. Both list eligible spend-down items. A gets the 2026 carryover arithmetic right ($680, so $1,220) and gives the formula $1,900 minus the carryover, which also covers a lower plan cap. It also asks for the exact grace end date and the incurred-versus-submitted deadlines. B blurs the 2026 figure into a $1,220–$1,240 range and a $1,240+ target, with no lower-cap arithmetic, and adds an unsourced \"~90 days\" run-out claim. B is more explicit that work after March 15 is not covered, and it adds the HSA/FSA caution. Its only nod to 2027 is generic advice to elect what you will spend, not the 2027 election for the March work, and A omits the 2027 point entirely. A is slightly more accurate, so it wins narrowly.
